content.thinking:
Since textures work fine under Node, I can run the build function via tsx to catch runtime errors, count parts, and compute bounding boxes. I'm planning a throwaway script that imports the sample, builds it, and checks geometry stats directly, since I can't visually inspect renders and need to rely on these numeric checks instead.

Writing the check script imports...

Finishing the hash function, then I'm defining a flame tongue function that uses sawtooth noise across an angular coordinate to produce layered flame bands (core, mid, outer) based on distance along the tongue, tapering each tongue's length toward its tip.

I'm checking that the core region lands near the base of each tongue and tapers to red tips, matching realistic flame coloring, then writing a side flame function that offsets the flame shape based on height and depth to position flames along the vehicle's sides, while noting that flames should only appear where the body side geometry actually exists.

For the hood, I'm using a mirrored absolute-value coordinate so flame tongues radiate symmetrically outward from the hood's centerline, then mapping that pattern onto the hood's top surface cells before starting to define the overall body paint function that samples cell position to decide coloring.

For mud, I'm blending noise with a vertical gradient so grime accumulates more toward the lower body and slightly toward the rear, with a threshold deciding where mud patches actually show up, then shading the splashes using a mud color ramp. Flame patterns only apply to the side faces and a specific hood region near the top, while the rest of the top surface stays plain orange.

Now I'm figuring out where flame decals are allowed to appear along the body, limiting them to the door-side region in z so they don't leak onto the bed. I'm also adding an outline by sampling neighboring texels and marking edges black wherever the flame level changes, then defining a four-step color ramp from red through orange to pale yellow for the flame gradient itself.

Then I'm shading the base coat using surface normals and a vertical gradient to pick the right ramp color, skipping separate seam details since those belong to other geometry, and adding sparse random rust specks. For the roof and trim I'm defining a dark paint ramp with dithering based on normal and noise, and starting on the chassis steel paint with speckled highlights and mud buildup logic.

Writing chrome and glass paint...

Still working out tire geometry...

Still defining tire texture layers...

Now I'm setting up each wheel to have its own paint variant across four slots, with tire and rim parts sharing a paint object, and sketching the wheel-building function that takes a hub position, orientation, and bone to construct the lathe geometry for the core.

Checking the rotation math confirms the lathe axis aligns correctly along x, then I'm working out the lug geometry—placing bolt-like boxes radially around the hub using trigonometry for position and rotating each box to align with the radial direction.

Chevron rows get alternating tilts of ±22° with staggered offsets between rows, and I'm counting out 22 lugs total, merging them with the tire paint. Now I'm thinking through how rim items get distributed per face.

Writing rim disc and bolt placement code...

Adding lug nuts and checking axial clearances so the tire, rim disc, and hub cap don't overlap with the body or shock mounts on either side.

Portal box and spindle placed at the axle end, mostly hidden by the teal disc, riding along the steer bone up front and axle at rear. Overall vehicle extents land at roughly ±1.95 in x, up to ~3.2 in y, and -2.7 to 2.9 in z. Now I'm setting up helper functions and type definitions for the body layout, starting with a color bag implementation.

Writing geometry transform and primitive helpers...

Writing cylinder tube geometry...

Actually I realize setFromUnitVectors is prohibited by the spec, so I should use the `aim` helper from the math module instead, which returns a quaternion pointing local y along a direction. Then for square-section bars, I'll build a similar function using BoxGeometry oriented with `aim(dir)` for frame pieces that need flat sides.

Now I'm also sketching out a decal helper for texture planes on bones, and planning the chassis layout: two steel rails as boxes with proper dimensions and position, built up from web and flange pieces to approximate a C-channel cross-section.

Adding lightening hole patterns...

Now I'm restricting the holes to only appear on the rail web surfaces by checking the x and y ranges, so axles and other painted parts stay unaffected. I'm planning to extend the frame rails further to the front, add kicked-up front horn extensions near the bumper, and place crossmembers at specific z positions.

Placing additional crossmembers along the frame with consistent dimensions, then working out the engine block's placement relative to the floor pan and rails -- checking that the engine bay floor is open where the block sits so it fits between the rails without clipping.

Now I'm building out the blower assembly: chrome housing, scoop with a dark intake face, a belt-drive pulley detail with a chrome cylinder and black ring, and header stacks, all positioned relative to the engine block before moving on to the hood.

Checking collisions between the hood opening and blower dimensions, I find the blower depth overlaps the hood's front/rear strips slightly, so I'm narrowing the blower to 0.5 deep and shortening the scoop to 0.36 to clear it. Now moving on to designing the fenders as boxes on either side.

Adding a grille facing forward on the front panel, then placing headlight pods on the fender fronts with black trim boxes around the lenses.

Adding hood side panels completes the hood geometry; I'm skipping scoops and trim but noting small chrome hood pins at corners. Now I'm starting the cab structure, defining the lower core box and firewall position using the body paint material.

Then I'm working out door and quarter panel placement: thin bodyPaint boxes offset slightly outward from the cab core to create a raised door-panel look, splitting the side into a door region and a rear quarter panel region.

Now I'm figuring out door edge detailing—creating a nested paint function where cells near the door border get a darker outline color while the rest resolves to bodyPaint, giving the panel seam a visible line.

I'm also roughing in the roof structure: a roof panel box with black trim, plus the A-pillar rods running from the cab shoulders up to the roofline, deciding whether to paint them orange like the body or black for contrast.

Now I'm working out the B-pillar and C-pillar placements along the door, sizing them as thin boxes and deciding on black trim paint so the roof reads as a darker band over the orange body.

Then I'm adding the quarter window glass between the pillars and the rear window glass, plus a back wall panel painted orange to tie the cab roof structure into the body color.

For the windshield, I'm computing a tilted box geometry sized and rotated to match the diagonal span from the cowl to the roofline, using the dz/dy offset to get the correct angle and length.

Now I'm adding the sun visor as a tilted box with a banner texture decal, then moving on to the doors—sizing each door skin's thickness, height, and depth, and positioning them symmetrically on either side of the vehicle.

I'm also planning a number decal for each door and the window frame net texture spanning between the pillars, plus a black window sill box positioned along the top rail.

Now I'm adding the door handle as a small chrome box, and defining the mirror as an arm bar connecting to a mirror body box.

Since the interior core box is solid below y=2.35, I only need visible seat parts above that line — so the driver seat back can be a box positioned near the belt line, with everything lower hidden inside the core.

I realize that making the whole cab a solid box causes problems: the top of the core would show as a flat orange plane inside the window openings, which looks wrong. I should instead build the cab hollow, with separate thin wall panels for the doors, firewall, floor, and rear, so the interior reads correctly through the windows.

Then I need to populate that hollow interior properly: seat bases and backs, driver figure, steering wheel, dash block with a sloped front, center console, shifter, and cage hoops, all fitted within the wall thicknesses I'm defining for the doors and rear wall.

Tilted back slightly, with a headrest added and seat paint done in black with teal piping accents. I'm placing the passenger seat mirrored, adding a center console between them, and starting the roll cage structure with vertical tubes behind the seats.

Still writing cage bars...

Computing the wheel's orientation basis vectors so I can draw the rim as an octagon positioned perpendicular to the steering column...

I'll skip the dash gauge decal, gear shifter, and fire extinguisher as low-value details, then move on to the bed: a dark liner-painted floor box and side wall boxes positioned along the truck bed frame.

Now I'm adding the wall top caps, front headboard wall behind the cab, and tailgate as additional trim-painted boxes completing the bed structure.

Then I'm positioning the tailgate between the side walls with chrome handle details, a hog-face decal facing outward, and considering small "MUD HOG" text on the bed sides, followed by the rear fender sill geometry.

Next I'm filling in the bed's lower body panel under the floor, extending it to the side walls and into the rear face below the gate. Then I'm adding a chrome rear bumper bar with uprights, a possible tow hitch ball, and small rear light boxes at the bed's rear corners.

For taillights, I'm placing them at the tailgate's outer edges with a pixel texture facing backward. Then I'm populating the bed with details -- nitro bottles, a toolbox, a red fuel can with handle, coiled rope -- and starting on the roll hoop with vertical tubes rising from the bed floor behind the cab.

For the hoop's light pods, I'm positioning four round lights across the top bar above the roof line, using circular planes with a pixel-ray texture for the lenses mounted on black cylindrical housings facing forward.

Then I'm placing chrome exhaust stacks behind the hoops with flared cap caps and base brackets, and designing the front bumper and bull bar assembly with chrome-black tube rails connecting the chassis to the bumper, a teal-accented winch box, red tow hooks, and a bull bar hoop extending from the bumper.

Keeping the bull bar simple with upright tubes capped by a top bar and diagonal braces, plus a pair of round fog lights and skipping the extra light bar since a roof lightbar already covers it. For the roof lightbar I'm building a black housing box with six forward-facing lens planes and mounting brackets.

Skipping the beacon and roof vent, I'll give the roof a black base with teal pinstripe edge lines, and add a small white "13" number decal painted flat on the roof surface.

Working out the orientation math for that roof text so it reads correctly when viewed from above and from the front...

On part count: merging might bring things to around 120 meshes, though vehicles need richer detail so I may want to keep more separate meshes for certain components rather than merging everything.

Now I'm working out the axle and suspension geometry — the axle tube dimensions, positioning the differential pumpkin as a cylinder along the z-axis, and figuring out steel paint treatments for these components per side.

Adding more shock mounts...

Still working out tower geometry...

Checking tire clearance against shock springs now — the spring radius at x~.97 slightly overlaps the tire inner face, so I'm shifting the shock x position inward and shrinking the spring radius slightly, but that creates a small intrusion into the front fender near the axle.

I'm also checking whether the lug geometry's rotated corners extend far enough inward to interfere with the shock body, accounting for the tilt angle adding a bit to the axial width.

Now I'm sketching the spring geometry as a sweep spiral with a given radius, height, and pitch, positioning it so the top clears the tower bar. Then I'm working out the lower control arm tubes, running from the axle lug up to a chassis mounting point on each side, trying to pick coordinates that make sense for the link angle toward the rail underside.

Next I'm adding upper control arms from the top of the axle to another chassis point, plus the steering tie rod connecting the two knuckles across the front axle, and basic driveshaft/U-joint placeholders before moving on to the brake rotor disc.

I'm sketching underbody details now—a skid plate under the engine and a battery box in the bed—then roughing out exhaust header stacks per side with curved pipe segments running along the chassis.

Writing header sweeps...

Checking clearances, I widen the hood opening slightly to keep header tubes clear of the side strips, then start thinking about an optional decal detail on top of the hood.

For the antenna, I'm running a thin tube from the bed corner upward to roughly y=3.7, which sets the overall model height, and planning a small checkered flag card at the tip using a thin plane.

Simpler plan: make the flag a thin box with the texture mapped onto it so all faces show the pattern. Now I'm thinking about adding the "MUD HOG" decal on the windshield and extra details like sponsor stickers and license plates on the tailgate.

For a racing-stripe look, I'll paint teal stripes along the bed sides by checking which faces fall in a specific z and y range on the body, coloring a couple thin bands teal/yellow to mimic a pinstripe.

I'm adding a "MUD HOG" decal centered on the tailgate wall, sized to fit within the bed side panel's y-range, plus planning a door number decal ("13") rendered as a small pixel-texture plane.

I'm designing a badge texture with a teal border, black fill, and white number text for the door decal, then moving on to figuring out the driver skin sheet dimensions, sizing the texture to fit the head region with a minimum width of 64 pixels.

Now I'm sketching out the helmet's pixel design: a white shell with a dark visor band and teal highlight on the front face, a teal stripe across the top, ear accents on the sides, and shading details like a chin bar row and highlight pixels on the visor.

Now I'm estimating total painted surface area across tires, lugs, rims, body, and chassis—roughly 130 m²—then calculating the texel density needed for a 2048 paint texture to cover that area at reasonable resolution.

Since the file is large, I'm planning to write it carefully in one pass, starting with type definitions and helper constants for angles and vectors. I'm setting up bag functions that collect geometry by material, then merging each bag's geometries at the end to create a single part with the right bone, position, and flat shading, while guarding against mismatched attribute sets between box, cylinder, and lathe geometries that could break the merge.

Now I'm working through flat shading behavior for faceted parts and confirming paints are baked correctly regardless of part-creation order. I'm writing the wheel-building function, which constructs a tire profile with a lathe geometry, rotates and translates it into position at the hub, and paints it using a tire-specific color function before adding it to the bone.

Writing lug placement code...

I'm now thinking about adding shoulder lugs near the tire's edge where the tread meets the sidewall, positioning angled boxes around axial ±0.4 and radial 0.76 so they wrap realistically beyond the sidewall at ±0.45.

With 22 lugs per row times 4 rows per wheel across 4 wheels, that's 352 boxes totaling around 4.2k triangles, which stays within budget. Now I'm building the rim face geometry, looping over both x directions to create a cylinder disc representing the outer face of the rim.

Adding bolt details, a hub cylinder, and nut boxes around the center...

Good, the rim disc pokes slightly past the sidewall at the right radius, confirming visibility. Now I'm writing the paint function for the teal disc, defining eight dark slots arranged in a ring pattern.

Adjusting the lighting formula so the top is brighter, then clamping values and setting the outer radius to a darker teal for the rim disc shading, before moving to chrome paint for the rim disc.

Merging the chrome and teal ramp logic into a single rim-paint helper keyed by local y/z coordinates, then setting flat chrome colors for the bolts, nuts, and hub cap, and skipping mud flap details for now.

Now I'm writing the pixel font definitions for the text builder, mapping letters to bitmap patterns.

Still writing font glyphs...

I'm sketching out a `textTex` function that converts a string into a small pixel texture, drawing a shadow offset by one pixel behind the foreground glyph color, and need to handle the width/height math carefully including the space character's blank pattern.

Now I'm planning out the full build function for the monster truck model, starting with a chassis joint and an axle joint positioned relative to it, before writing out the rest of the geometry code.

Still writing joint hierarchy...

I'm realizing I need to check whether placing the steering and wheel joints at the exact same hub position as their parent creates zero-length bones, which could be a problem worth catching before moving on.

Door joints with zero bone length are fine since they're leaf joints with no children. Now I'm confirming part options like flat rendering are supported, then starting to set up decal planes for surface details.

For the decal orientation, I'm working through the cross-product math to verify that a decal placed on the front face with up [0,1,0] correctly aligns its local X axis with world X, matching what a viewer standing in front would see as "right" on the model — getting into the coordinate geometry to make sure the texture doesn't end up mirrored.

For the back face, I'm checking the same cross product and confirming the local X axis flips to -X world, which again matches a viewer standing behind looking forward.

Now I'm sketching out pixel textures for details like the grille and headlights, defining small pixel-art patterns with palette colors for frame, lens, and highlight regions.

Designing the taillight texture...

Still working out the window opening dimensions...

I'll place that plane at y 2.65, z 0.33 to fit the door bone. For the grille texture, I'm drawing a dark background with chrome bars across the rows and a teal vertical divider, skipping the badge and dash gauge details, then moving on to sidewall and mud paint passes.

I need to check that chassis rail components merge correctly under the chassis bone and paint color, confirm the steering wheel tube positions are set in model-space, and verify mergeGeometries will work since box and cylinder attribute sets align properly. Now I'm setting wheel positions and starting to write out the full palette and geometry code.

Writing palette constants...

Now I'm defining mud color variants and a helper to compute mud buildup based on height on the vehicle, then building the body paint function that samples cell position and normal to decide between flame patterns, edge outlines, and bed stripe regions on the side panels and hood.

I'm checking whether flames might unintentionally bleed onto interior wall faces or other hidden geometry, but concluding it's fine since those surfaces aren't typically visible, and now I'm layering mud splatter effects on top of the flame patterns near the bottom using a noise-based score.

Now I'm restricting mud to non-top-facing surfaces and adding a special hood flame detail that only kicks in under specific position and normal conditions, then moving on to roof trim paint and door panel line details based on proximity to door edges.

Still defining door edge cells...

I'll place a number badge on the door above the flame decal, and skip extra fender text. For the header sweep I'm defining bezier curves with chrome and burnt-metal color bands along a six-sided tube with flat caps.

For the springs, I'm sweeping a four-sided coil along a spiral path around the axle, setting turns, pitch, and radius to shape the geometry, with the spiral starting at the axle height and climbing along its axis.

For the antenna I'll use a simple tube. For the flag, I'm creating a small teal-and-white checkered texture and applying it to a thin box geometry extending backward from the mast, positioning it near the rear of the vehicle. I also need to add an interior steering shaft running as a tube from the dashboard point toward the steering wheel's center.

I'm now double-checking that everything touches the ground properly—verifying the tires' lug nuts sit flush at y=0 despite their rotation, accounting for the slight corner offset introduced by tilting the lug boxes along the radial axis.

Confirming front and rear body extents are symmetric, and mapping the mirror layout so the driver's side sits at +x for a US-style build. Now I'm moving on to writing the actual code and figuring out decal placement positions on the surface.

Writing full build code...

Still writing geometry helpers and paint functions for the chrome and steel parts, with a sparkle effect based on surface normals for the chrome shader.

Now I'm working out the placement of bed items: nitro bottles with chrome valves and strap boxes, plus a toolbox positioned near the back of the bed, calibrating their exact coordinates and dimensions.

Adding more bed objects...

Keeping antenna height around 3.7, matching the roll bar lights at 3.5, which lines up with a real truck height near 3.6 meters. I'm deciding against adding extra details like rocker trim boxes or wheel well arches since the tires sit outboard, but I'm still weighing whether to add grille guard lights or hood details up front.

Confirming the front is properly closed between the fenders with the front panel spanning the gap, checking the grille plane position and width against the fender boundaries, and placing headlight bezels at the fender fronts with appropriately centered lens dimensions. Skipping the front splitter/valence idea and finalizing the hood trim paint for the sides before writing it out.

input.command: sed -n 1,60p src/parts.ts; grep -n "flat" src/parts.ts | head; grep -n "texture" src/parts.ts | head
